opus-5.5.text:
I think the healthiest way to see it is as co-evolution rather than one side leading the other. People sometimes talk about the "hardware lottery" — the idea that the algorithms that win are often the ones that happen to fit the hardware we already have. The Transformer is a good example. It's not necessarily the most elegant architecture in some abstract sense, but it maps extremely well onto GPUs: big dense matrix multiplications, lots of parallelism, very regular memory access. That fit is a huge part of why it scaled and why it won.

So from my perspective, working on inference systems, I'd say algorithm designers really benefit from understanding hardware constraints, at least at the level of intuition. What's compute-bound versus memory-bound, how expensive data movement is compared to arithmetic, what happens to utilization when your batch is small. A lot of recent architectural innovations — grouped-query attention, multi-head latent attention, mixture-of-experts, various quantization schemes — are really responses to hardware realities. During decoding, for instance, you're often bottlenecked by memory bandwidth reading the KV cache, not by FLOPs. If you design an attention variant that shrinks the KV cache, you get a real-world speedup even if the theoretical FLOP count barely changes.

In the other direction, hardware is a very slow, very expensive bet. A chip takes years from design to deployment, so hardware designers have to guess where models will be two or three years out. If they over-specialize — say, hard-wiring for one particular attention pattern — and the field moves, that silicon becomes much less useful. That's why I think hardware should mostly invest in robust primitives: high memory bandwidth, large and fast interconnects, flexible low-precision formats, good support for sparsity and irregular workloads like MoE routing. Those bets tend to stay valuable no matter which specific architecture is in fashion.

And in between there's the software layer, which I think is underrated. Systems like vLLM, compilers, kernel libraries — this is where you absorb the mismatch between what the model wants and what the hardware offers. A good software stack lets algorithm people experiment without each of them becoming a CUDA expert, and lets hardware vendors plug in without rewriting the whole ecosystem. In a sense, the software layer is what makes co-design practical at scale.

So my short answer: algorithms should be hardware-aware, hardware should be trend-aware but not over-fitted, and the systems layer in the middle should make both sides' lives easier. The biggest gains in the last few years have come from people who were willing to think across those boundaries instead of staying in one box.

r001.rationale: It says hardware is a slow, expensive bet, chips take years from design to deployment, and an over-specialized chip can lose usefulness if the field moves.

r002.rationale: It describes recent architecture choices as responses to hardware realities, while hardware invests in robust primitives because it takes years to develop. This communicates that adaptation happens more on the algorithm and architecture side.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's a two-way street, and right now the traffic flows much more heavily in one direction than people admit.

Historically, hardware led. The Transformer won not because it was the most elegant idea, but because it was the architecture that happened to map almost perfectly onto what GPUs were good at: big dense matrix multiplications, very regular memory access, lots of parallelism. Recurrent models were arguably more "natural" for sequences, but they were sequential, and sequential is exactly what a GPU hates. So in a sense the hardware picked the winner. The same thing is happening again with things like FlashAttention, or with MoE. Those are algorithmic ideas, but the reason they matter is that they respect the memory hierarchy. They're really about moving fewer bytes, not doing fewer FLOPs.

So the first thing I'd say to anyone designing models is: you need to understand roofline. You need to know whether you're compute-bound or memory-bound, what your arithmetic intensity is, how big the KV cache is at the batch sizes you'll actually serve. A lot of papers propose architectures that look great on a FLOPs count and then are two or three times slower in practice, because the operations don't fuse, or because they introduce dependencies that break the pipeline. Working on inference systems, I see this constantly. The gap between "theoretically cheaper" and "actually faster" is where most ideas die.

But I don't think algorithms should just passively adapt. The other direction matters too, and it has a longer time constant. Hardware takes three to five years to design and ship, so the chips we're getting now were designed around the models of 2021 or 2022. That's why we see things like dedicated support for lower-precision formats, FP8 and now FP4, or bigger on-chip SRAM, or faster interconnect. Those are hardware responding to what the algorithms community showed was useful. Quantization research pushed the hardware; the hardware then made quantization the default.

The risk in this loop is lock-in. If hardware is optimized for Transformers, and new architectures are evaluated on hardware optimized for Transformers, then anything structurally different looks bad, and we never find out whether it would have been better. State-space models are a good example. Are they really worse, or are they just less optimized? It took a lot of kernel engineering before you could even make a fair comparison. So I think the field has to deliberately leave some room for ideas that don't fit today's chips, otherwise we converge on a local optimum.

Where I think the right relationship is heading is co-design, but at a level of abstraction that's higher than it is now. Today, co-design means a few very talented people hand-writing CUDA kernels. That doesn't scale. What we need are compilers and serving systems that let a researcher express an idea and get something reasonably efficient automatically, so that the feedback loop between "I have an idea" and "I know what it costs" is hours, not months. That's a big part of why I care about open-source inference infrastructure. If the systems layer is open and flexible, then algorithms can evolve faster, and the hardware people get a clearer signal about what to build next.

So, short version: hardware sets the constraints, algorithms explore within them, and the best work happens when the people on each side actually talk to each other, rather than throwing things over the wall.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware takes three to five years to design and ship, and describes the resulting risk of lock-in when hardware is optimized for current architectures. This communicates that a mistaken hardware direction can persist for years.

r002.rationale: The response calls the relationship a two-way street but says traffic currently flows more heavily one way, explains how architectures adapt to GPU strengths, and summarizes that hardware sets constraints while algorithms explore within them.

astra-6.text:
I think they should evolve together. When we design an algorithm or a model architecture, we should consider how it actually runs on hardware. Fewer operations don’t necessarily mean lower latency. You also have to consider memory access, communication, and how much parallelism the hardware can exploit.

At the same time, we shouldn’t treat today’s hardware as a permanent constraint. New algorithms can reveal opportunities for better hardware design. So it’s a feedback loop: hardware capabilities inform model design, and the needs of models inform the next generation of hardware. Ultimately, we should evaluate the whole system—what quality can we achieve, at what latency and cost?

r001.rationale: The response discusses hardware and model co-evolution but does not say that a wrong hardware-development decision can persist for several years.

r002.rationale: The response describes a two-way feedback loop, without stating that practical adaptation happens more on the algorithm and architecture side.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they should evolve together. When we design an algorithm or a model architecture, we should consider how efficiently it can run on real hardware, not just how many theoretical operations it requires. Memory access, communication, and parallelism can matter just as much as computation.

At the same time, hardware development should respond to what algorithms actually need. There’s a balance: if we optimize hardware too narrowly for today’s architectures, we may limit tomorrow’s ideas. So I’d like to see a feedback loop, where researchers and hardware designers work closely together, while leaving enough flexibility for new approaches.

r001.rationale: The response discusses balancing hardware choices with future ideas, but does not say that a wrong hardware-development turn can persist for several years.

r002.rationale: It calls for a feedback loop and says hardware should respond to algorithm needs, but does not state that adaptation in practice happens more on the algorithm and architecture side.
